Figure 1:Robot-use interfaces (RUIs) shape embodied agent performance.Top:RUIKit organizes six action abstractions and two interaction forms into 13 RUIs under shared perception and control.Bottom:(a) Interface choice substantially affects agent success.
(b) Decision compression and in-program feedback provide complementary gains.
(c) Interface preferences shift from simulation to reality.
(d) RUI-specific fine-tuning improves small-model performance in both interaction forms.

Figure 2:The 30 tasks of RUIBench.Each row is a suite of six simulated tasks, defined by what success requires: reasoning from prior knowledge, using previously shown visual examples, physical exploration, responding to time-sensitive events, or precise adjustments during contact.
The right column shows the task of each suite that also runs on the real robot.

Figure 3:Overview of RUIKit.The RUI is the only variable for a fixed agent and task, while the harness, 24 underlying tools, evaluation protocol, and robot backend remain shared.
The scorer’s verdict is withheld from the agent.

Figure 4:Real-robot rollouts on the first layout.Each row shows four frames of one episode from the third-person camera.
On the same task and layout, Claude Code topples the whole chain with per-action Delta (a), but only the blue domino falls, sideways, after its program (b).
Per-action episodes also recover from a beam that lands beside its supports (c) and a cube that rests tilted on the lid (d).

Figure 5:Illusory completion in simulation.Each column crops the last camera image returned to the agent before it calledtask_done, and the red circle marks the failure that the judge names.
Codex notes the fallen piece yet reports the goal as reached, whereas the same model, given only these images in a fresh context, recognizes the failure: observing a failure does not guarantee recognizing it.

Figure 6:Simulated rollouts: World Knowledge.One successful episode per task on the first test mission, seen from the camera that the agent itself observes (the fixed camera, or the head camera for two-arm tasks).

Figure 7:Simulated rollouts: In-Context Learning.One successful episode per task on the first test mission, seen from the camera that the agent itself observes (the fixed camera, or the head camera for two-arm tasks).

Figure 8:Simulated rollouts: Discovery.One successful episode per task on the first test mission, seen from the camera that the agent itself observes (the fixed camera, or the head camera for two-arm tasks).

Figure 9:Simulated rollouts: Dynamic Interaction.One successful episode per task on the first test mission, seen from the camera that the agent itself observes (the fixed camera, or the head camera for two-arm tasks).

Figure 10:Simulated rollouts: Contact-Rich Manipulation.One successful episode per task on the first test mission, seen from the camera that the agent itself observes (the fixed camera, or the head camera for two-arm tasks). Fold the T-Shirt (CR6) has no successful episode on this mission.

Figure 11:Real-robot rollouts: correcting placements.Each row shows four frames of one episode on the first layout, from the third-person camera, together with its task, agent, RUI, and number of replies. The agents inspect what they have placed and adjust it until the arrangement works.

Figure 12:Real-robot rollouts: contact and hand pose.Each row shows four frames of one episode on the first layout, from the third-person camera, together with its task, agent, RUI, and number of replies. The agents push stuck or tilted pieces into their holes and turn or tilt the hand to suit the object and the target.

Figure 13:Real-robot rollouts: programs and search.Each row shows four frames of one episode on the first layout, from the third-person camera, together with its task, agent, RUI, and number of replies. Claude Code’s programs compose several actions per reply (a, b), and a program episode can still correct its own work (c).
